en: His right shoulder blade was broad,
All twelve members evenly formed;
This blood-drinker, utterly different,
Was a lion who would shatter the Oirat.
Should a giant tall as a mountain rise,
Without shrinking back or closing his eyes,
He looked ready to charge it;
Making roads of ninety mountains,
He looked ready to cross them.
Throwing the world into turmoil,
He looked ready to trample it;
With an iron shield, in steel,
He looked ready to arm himself;
Against the eighteen thousand worlds
He looked ready to strike.
Leaving Talas behind,
The leopard beloved of God
Showed his blood-drinking aspect.
He was their sultan, he their support;
For the few people who suffered hardship,
He was the lion they trusted.
Formidable in cunning, fierce in wrath,
For these few Kyrgyz people
He was the strength they leaned upon.
The generous lord left Talas,
Riding his swift dun steed;
Your blue-maned lord that day
Was seeking out his kin.
Since he himself was a hero,
Would he stop before finding his kin?
“Having found his kin safe and sound,
Will the blood-drinker return?” they said.
“Before the blood-drinker comes back,
Will they overwhelm us, ah,
Those swarming, deceitful Chinese?” they said.
“There are many gray, hilly mountains;
Without our mountain-like blood-drinker,
There are many foes to cause upheaval.
Before Manas returns,
Before he sees his people safe,
If a shouting enemy rises,
If some terrible trouble arises,
Generous Manas is not here—
What will become of our lives?” they said.
Old women wept, old men grieved:
“Dark mountains surround us;
Talas is the land for us.
Letting no winged creature strike us,
Letting no whip-bearer beat us,
Blood-drinking Manas was the hero
Who could care for these people.
If this Manas does not return,
What enemy will devour us?!”
His people grieved, thinking this:
“The leopard born a noble falcon
Was our shelter and our support.
Away from Black Kalmyks and Manchus
He moved us, safe and sound;
He was the hero who brought us here.
Until he turns and comes back,
Until he sees his people's faces,
May my Manas be safe,
May my Talas lie at ease!
Creator, if you created him to live,
Let him make Keng-Kol and Talas his home;
Keep generous Manas safe!
If Manas lives safe and sound,
We shall see some happiness.
If Manas closes his eyes,
We shall all die together!
Amen!” they said, spreading their palms;
Such were his people's thoughts.
God's sun grew clouded in the sky;
All the people left behind
Had sixty worries come upon them at once.
At the age of twelve
He stormed palaces and took booty—
Could there be another such hero?
Could the hero granted them by fate,
Going forth, leave his own people
Without concern for them?
He was a champion and a support;
Ah, blue-maned lion Manas—
He was a hero granted them by fortune.
Your blue-maned one, visited by Kydyr,
Is going to a precious place.
If he vanishes and does not return,
Our fortune will tilt awry;
Nothing like it happens in an age!
As though parting forever,
Sobbing out their sorrow,
“We shall not see him now,” they said;
The simple people cried aloud.
Told to drink water, he drank poison;
Told to take a cap, he cut off a head;
Told to spill blood, he spilled rage.
Flourishing whenever depleted,
He was Manas, the deep-rooted lion;
Growing stronger whenever he died,
He was Manas, the keen-edged hero.
Before one could circle a sheepfold,
Where he had made his camp
A sheepfold's worth of red willows grew.
For the lord protected by Kozhosan,
Holy Kydyr became a helper.
Where he had passed the night,
A deep-rooted plane tree took hold.
The enemies who challenged him
Were all utterly destroyed;
Not one of them remained alive.
The keen hero visited by Kydyr
Behaved differently from all men.
When roused to rage and fury,
The peerless one shook the world.
The leopard grew wrathful;
Keen Manas would not stop.
Readying himself like a lion,
The dear hero born to fortune
Mounted and set out from Talas.
The horse he rode was Akkula;
He girded on an unsheathed sword.
The dear hero sought his kin,
Like a cloud about to rain again;
Toward the world's four corners,
Wrath spreading over his face,
To look about on every side,
Lord Manas did not stop.
To find his kin,
He now crossed Zhorgonun-Bel.
Over yellow, uneven ridges
Your blue-maned Manas rode now.
When he descended the other side,
Yellow rolling hills came into view.
Murmuring through the ravines,
Springs poured out by the thousand.
Looking closely, this place
Seemed the choicest of lands.
From this land's river valley
A breeze came caressing the face.
Ah, dear one, this land
Was a place a mortal would long for.
Looking toward the level ground,
With their tails flung outward,
Wild asses raced at play.
In this land's hills
Bears wrestled, baring their teeth.
If you looked into its hollows,
Springs flowed and overflowed.
From sheltered nook after nook,
Nightingales sang and trilled.
Hearing the nightingale's voice,
A sorrowful mortal softened to tears.
Crossing ridge after rounded ridge,
Marveling at the land he saw,
Manas grew excited and glad.
The wild game in the hills
Bounded at play, raising dust.
Along the level ground in lines,
Foxes trailed their tails;
Loping on the lower slopes,
Wolves showed their reddened eyes.
The hilly parts of this land
Held gray hares and foxes.
This Sary Özön here
Was the treasure of all the earth.
They would call it the choicest of lands;
All the holy elders were there;
It was a land where saints would walk,
That was why they called this land
Oluya-Ata.
True saints and holy elders,
Those with ragged clothes and hungry bellies,
Would make this land their home.
Sorrow, grief, and humiliation
Would disappear in this land.
Poor and helpless people
Would prosper in this land.
Below it lay a hot desert;
Its lower slopes were golden land.
Was it not the choicest of lands?
Would not a mortal settled there find peace?
For those who made and kept a home,
It was a place of refuge.
Those who settled there securely,
Taking horse-belly fat a span thick,
Would grow rich in this land.
Rejoicing at the land he saw,
The blue-maned leopard grew excited.
The blue-maned one, the outstanding hero,
To the yellow, uneven hills,
To Zhangyryk's Zhar-Kyya,
To the trail for a single horse,
To the rugged mountain neck,
The generous lord now came.
Across the moon-bright yellow plain,
His attention was caught by a sight:
As huge as half a mountain,
As though he would devour whoever he met,
With a tiger's gaze,
Leaving no challenger alive,
With the look of a cold fog,
With the eyes of a true devourer,
Bull-necked, stallion-camel-thighed,
Wearing out all who grappled with him,
His ears like a vest, like a shield—
If you looked at his mustache,
Like nettles growing on an old camp site—
A man emerged over the ridge.
His nose like a mountain spur,
Biting right through his lip,
His two eyes deeply sunken,
Seething far within.
He rode a gray horse fit to be a tulpar;
He wore a coat of blue iron.
His heroism was extraordinary,
His blue-maned valor immeasurable.
He wore a cap of gray lynx fur;
A blue-mottled shield swung about.
Wrath spread over his face.
A cast-iron mace of twelve batman
Was fastened at his right side.
He wore out horses, scouting the land;
He loosed hounds and flew hawks;
He wore an unsheathed sword.
With the aspect of a lion,
Wrath spread over his countenance.
His dangling eyelashes
Were like the handle of a greasy axe.
Seeing Bakay's valor,
Your hero Manas marveled.
“Ever since Manas became Manas,
Ever since Manas took to horseback,
Since my dear father Jakyp pursued me,
Since my hapless mother Chyyrdy bore me—
I was born in Altay and grew mighty.
I grew seasoned by spilling blood;
Thrusting my spear, breaking crowds,
Among the swarming Chinese
I earned the name blood-drinking Burut.
I saw mighty men, I saw lions;
I met all manner of giants as equals.
Among heroes I have seen none like him.
I routed governors, humiliating them;
Of their strong men wearing armored vests,
I speared many by force.
I have not met my death and died;
I have never seen such a being.
Riding alone, scouting the land,
Striking those he reaches, taking booty—
Is he one of the monsters?
Shouting battle cries, his spear
He looks a man who would thrust,
Slaughter upon the world
He is a man who would bring.
As huge as half a mountain,
As though he would devour a soul he met,
